title: Basics of Organic Chemistry
scope: A 60-level foundation-to-MSc bridge with continued practice required; not a promise of full MSc mastery.

curriculum.title: Carbon starts with four bonds
curriculum.question: How can one element make so many different molecules?
curriculum.plain_language: Think of a bond as a shared pair of electrons. In methane, carbon shares one pair with each of four hydrogens. Carbon can also bond to other carbons, making chains, branches and rings. A drawing is a record of these connections, not a picture of atoms touching like solid balls.
curriculum.reasoning: A neutral carbon with four ordinary bonds has eight electrons around it when shared electrons are counted for both bonded atoms. One double bond counts as two bonds. Always check the total bond order before adding a hidden hydrogen.
curriculum.worked_example: CH4: four C–H bonds. In CH2=CH2 each carbon has a double bond and two C–H bonds: total bond order four.
curriculum.advanced_connection: The octet is a useful starting model, not a universal law for every intermediate. Carbocations, radicals and carbenes need separate electron counts. Later levels explain why those species react.

checks.question: How many ordinary bonds does neutral carbon have in methane?
checks.explanation: Carbon shares four pairs in CH4.

checks.question: In CH2=CH2, the C=C contributes what bond order at each carbon?
checks.explanation: A double bond counts twice when checking valence.

checks.question: Why can carbon form long molecular chains?
options: It bonds to other carbon atoms
It must always form an ion
checks.answer: It bonds to other carbon atoms
checks.explanation: Carbon–carbon bonding permits chains and branches.

curriculum.title: Read the invisible carbons
curriculum.question: Where did the C and H labels disappear to?
curriculum.plain_language: In a skeletal drawing, an unlabelled line end or corner represents carbon. A line is a bond. Hydrogens attached to carbon are usually omitted; add enough to give that carbon its normal valence. Atoms such as O and N are written explicitly.
curriculum.reasoning: Read connections before guessing a name. A zigzag with three connected lines contains four carbon positions. A bend is not an extra bond floating in space. Double and triple lines change how many hydrogens can attach.
curriculum.worked_example: A three-segment unbranched zigzag is butane, C4H10. CH3–CH2–OH has two carbons even though an oxygen appears at one end.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Explicit charges and heteroatom hydrogens matter. Do not silently turn a charged atom into a neutral atom while counting. Stereochemical wedges describe spatial orientation, not additional atoms.

checks.question: An unlabelled endpoint in a skeletal structure normally means what?
checks.explanation: Endpoints and corners represent carbon unless labelled otherwise.

checks.question: How many carbons are in a three-segment unbranched zigzag?
checks.explanation: Count both endpoints and the two internal corners.

checks.question: Which atoms are normally written explicitly?
checks.explanation: Heteroatoms must remain visible in skeletal drawings.

curriculum.title: Find the functional group
curriculum.question: Why do two similar carbon chains behave differently?
curriculum.plain_language: A functional group is a recognisable arrangement of atoms that strongly affects a molecule’s reactions. An alcohol contains an O–H group attached to a saturated carbon. A carbonyl contains C=O. An alkene contains C=C. Start by circling these groups before naming an entire molecule.
curriculum.reasoning: The neighbourhood matters. An O–H directly attached to a carbonyl carbon belongs to a carboxylic acid. Oxygen between two carbons makes an ether. Identifying a group is the beginning of reasoning, not a promise that every molecule with it reacts identically.
curriculum.worked_example: Ethanol: CH3CH2OH, an alcohol. Ethanal: CH3CHO, an aldehyde. Ethanoic acid: CH3CO2H, a carboxylic acid.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Functional groups interact through conjugation, steric effects and acid–base chemistry. A synthesis plan often changes one group selectively while leaving another intact. That selectivity becomes a major theme later.

checks.question: Which bond identifies a carbonyl group?
checks.explanation: The carbon–oxygen double bond is the defining feature.

checks.question: CH3CH2OH belongs to which class?
checks.explanation: Its hydroxyl group is attached to saturated carbon.

checks.question: CH3CO2H contains which functional group?
checks.explanation: The OH and C=O belong to the same carboxyl group.

curriculum.title: Keep track of charge
curriculum.question: How can oxygen be positive and carbon be negative?
curriculum.plain_language: Formal charge is an accounting tool. Give an atom all its lone-pair electrons and half its bonding electrons, then compare that count with the neutral atom’s valence electrons. A charge symbol must follow the electrons; it is not chosen to make a mechanism look convenient.
curriculum.reasoning: For common oxygen drawings: two bonds and two lone pairs is neutral; three bonds and one lone pair gives +1; one bond and three lone pairs gives −1. A charged atom can still be part of a molecule whose total charge is zero.
curriculum.worked_example: H3O+ has positively charged oxygen. HO− has negatively charged oxygen. H2O has neutral oxygen. Proton transfer interconverts these electron-count patterns.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Formal charge does not measure the full physical distribution of charge. Polar bonds have partial charges even when both atoms have formal charge zero. Check total charge on both sides of every mechanism step.

checks.question: Oxygen with three single bonds and one lone pair has which formal charge?
checks.explanation: It is assigned five electrons rather than its neutral six.

checks.question: What must a valid reaction step conserve?
options: The number of drawn lone pairs on each atom
The charge on every individual atom
checks.explanation: Charges may move, but total charge is conserved.

checks.question: Does formal charge describe every partial charge in a polar bond?
checks.explanation: Formal and partial charge describe different aspects of bonding.

curriculum.title: Build a molecule on paper
curriculum.question: Can you check a structure before memorising its name?
curriculum.plain_language: Use a repeatable order: find the carbon skeleton, identify functional groups, add hidden hydrogens and check charges. Then count the molecular formula. This turns a complicated picture into several small checks that you can actually explain.
curriculum.reasoning: For ordinary neutral closed-shell compounds containing C, H, N and halogens, DBE = (2C + 2 + N − H − X)/2. Oxygen does not appear in this expression. A ring or double bond contributes one DBE; a triple bond contributes two.
curriculum.worked_example: C2H6O has DBE zero. Ethanol and dimethyl ether both fit it. C2H4O has DBE one, which could represent a ring or a double bond.
curriculum.advanced_connection: DBE is a constraint, not a structure solver. Different isomers can have the same formula and DBE. Charged species, radicals and unusual valences require extra care rather than blind substitution into this rule.

checks.question: What is the DBE of neutral C2H6O?
A triple bond contributes how many DBE?
checks.explanation: Its two additional bond orders contribute two unsaturations.

checks.question: Does molecular formula plus DBE uniquely identify every structure?
checks.explanation: Isomers can satisfy exactly the same formula and DBE.

curriculum.title: Sigma, pi and shape
curriculum.question: Why is a double bond difficult to twist?
curriculum.plain_language: A sigma bond overlaps along the line between two nuclei. A pi bond comes from sideways overlap of p orbitals. A double bond has one sigma and one pi bond. Rotating its two ends would spoil that sideways overlap, so it is not freely rotatable like an isolated single bond.
curriculum.reasoning: The common shapes are tetrahedral around sp3 carbon, approximately trigonal planar around sp2 carbon and linear around sp carbon. Hybridisation is a model that helps connect bonding, shape and orbital overlap.
curriculum.worked_example: Ethene: each carbon is sp2 and has one unhybridised p orbital. Ethyne: each carbon is sp; its triple bond contains one sigma and two pi bonds.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Conjugated systems require aligned p orbitals across neighbouring atoms. Planarity and orientation therefore influence reactivity. Count sigma and pi bonds separately before applying orbital language to a reaction.

checks.question: A carbon–carbon double bond contains what?
options: One sigma and one pi bond
checks.answer: One sigma and one pi bond
checks.explanation: One overlap lies along the axis and one lies sideways.

checks.question: What is the usual geometry of an sp carbon?
checks.explanation: Two sp orbitals point in opposite directions.

checks.question: Why is ordinary C=C rotation restricted?
options: The sigma bond always breaks first
checks.explanation: The p orbitals must remain aligned for pi bonding.

curriculum.title: Polar bonds point the way
curriculum.question: Which end of a carbonyl attracts an electron pair?
curriculum.plain_language: Bonded atoms do not always share electrons equally. Oxygen attracts electron density strongly, so a carbonyl is polar: oxygen is relatively electron-rich and its carbon relatively electron-poor. These partial charges help you predict where another molecule may attack.
curriculum.reasoning: Write δ+ and δ− for partial charges. Do not replace them with full + and − formal charges without changing the electron count. A molecule can have polar bonds but little overall dipole if its bond dipoles cancel by symmetry.
curriculum.worked_example: In R2C=O, a nucleophile commonly attacks carbon. The C=O pi pair moves to oxygen during ordinary nucleophilic addition.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Electronegativity alone is not a complete reactivity rule. Resonance, solvent, steric access and orbital energies also matter. Use polarity to propose an attack site, then check the complete mechanism.

checks.question: Which atom of a simple carbonyl is usually electrophilic?
checks.explanation: The C=O bond is polarised towards oxygen.

checks.question: What does δ+ mean?
checks.explanation: Partial charges describe uneven electron density.

checks.question: Can bond dipoles cancel in a symmetrical molecule?
options: Only if all bonds are nonpolar
checks.explanation: The molecular dipole is a vector sum.

curriculum.title: Resonance is one molecule
curriculum.question: Does benzene switch between two drawings?
curriculum.plain_language: Resonance contributors are alternative electron-bookkeeping drawings of the same molecular arrangement. The atoms stay in the same places. The real species has delocalised electron density; it is not rapidly hopping between separate structures.
curriculum.reasoning: Move lone pairs or pi electrons while keeping the sigma framework and total charge unchanged. Every contributor must obey valid valence rules. Use a resonance double-headed arrow, not an equilibrium arrow between different compounds.
curriculum.worked_example: Acetate has two equivalent contributors with the negative charge drawn on either oxygen. The real charge is distributed over the carboxylate group.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Contributors need not have equal weight. Octets, charge separation and electronegativity help judge their importance. Equivalent contributors explain equivalent bonds, as in the two C–O bonds of a carboxylate.

checks.question: What changes between resonance contributors?
checks.explanation: The same atoms retain the same connectivity.

checks.question: Does a resonance arrow mean two compounds are in equilibrium?
checks.explanation: A resonance hybrid is one species.

checks.question: Why are acetate’s C–O bonds equivalent in its delocalised structure?
options: Both bonds are isolated single bonds
checks.explanation: Equivalent electron distributions contribute to one hybrid.

curriculum.title: Make the arrows make sense
curriculum.question: Why must an arrow start from electrons?
curriculum.plain_language: A full curved arrow represents movement of an electron pair. Its tail begins at a lone pair or a bond. Its head shows the atom or bond receiving that pair. Begin with an electron source, not with the atom you hope will react.
curriculum.reasoning: For HO− attacking CH3Br, draw one arrow from an oxygen lone pair to carbon and another from the C–Br bond to bromine. Both belong to one concerted SN2 step. Carbon cannot keep all its old bonds and gain a fifth full bond.
curriculum.worked_example: HO− + CH3Br → CH3OH + Br−. Donor pair: oxygen lone pair. Departing pair: C–Br bond. Net charge stays −1.
curriculum.advanced_connection: A fishhook arrow tracks one electron and belongs in radical mechanisms. Arrow pushing must preserve atoms and charge and respect the relevant octet rules. An arrow is a mechanistic claim that needs chemical justification.

checks.question: Where should an electron-pair arrow begin?
options: At a bond or lone pair
checks.answer: At a bond or lone pair
checks.explanation: An arrow tracks electrons from their source.

checks.question: During C–Br heterolysis, where does the bonding pair go?
checks.explanation: Bromide receives the pair.

checks.question: A fishhook arrow represents what?
checks.explanation: Single-electron steps use fishhook arrows.

curriculum.title: Acid and base are roles
curriculum.question: Why can water accept a proton in one reaction and donate one in another?
curriculum.plain_language: A Brønsted acid donates a proton; a Brønsted base accepts one. Water can do either depending on its reaction partner. These names describe a role in a particular reaction, not an unchangeable label for a bottle.
curriculum.reasoning: When a base accepts H+, the acid’s X–H bonding pair stays on X. Draw an arrow from the base’s lone pair to H and a second from X–H to X. The donor becomes its conjugate base; the acceptor becomes its conjugate acid.
curriculum.worked_example: NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + HO−. Ammonia accepts H+; water donates it in this direction.
curriculum.advanced_connection: A Lewis base donates an electron pair and a Lewis acid accepts one. This broader definition includes interactions without proton transfer. Keep proton transfer separate from electron-transfer redox chemistry.

checks.question: A Brønsted base does what?
checks.explanation: Accepting H+ defines its role.

checks.question: When HA loses H+, where does the H–A pair remain?
checks.explanation: Deprotonation leaves the bonding pair on the conjugate base.

checks.question: A Lewis base donates what?
checks.explanation: Lewis acid–base chemistry is electron-pair donation and acceptance.

curriculum.title: Use pKa to choose a direction
curriculum.question: Can two numbers tell you which side a proton prefers?
curriculum.plain_language: pKa describes acid strength in a specified medium. Smaller pKa means a stronger acid. Compare the acid on each side of a proton-transfer equilibrium; the side with the weaker acid is usually favoured.
curriculum.reasoning: For HA + B− ⇌ A− + HB, a useful estimate is log10 K ≈ pKa(HB) − pKa(HA), using values on a compatible solvent scale. A positive difference favours products. Concentrations and solvent still matter.
curriculum.worked_example: If HA has pKa 5 and HB has pKa 10 on the same scale, K is approximately 10^5 for the reaction as written.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Do not mix aqueous pKa values with values measured in DMSO and expect a precise equilibrium constant. Approximate comparisons are valuable when their assumptions are explicit.

checks.question: Which acid is stronger on the same pKa scale?
checks.explanation: Lower pKa means a stronger acid.

checks.question: For pKa(HA)=5 and pKa(HB)=10, approximate K is what?
checks.explanation: Use 10 raised to 10−5.

checks.question: Why avoid mixing pKa values from unrelated solvents?
options: They are not directly comparable scales
checks.answer: They are not directly comparable scales
checks.explanation: Solvation affects the measured equilibria.

curriculum.title: Stabilise the conjugate base
curriculum.question: Why is a carboxylic acid more acidic than an alcohol?
curriculum.plain_language: After an acid gives up H+, inspect what remains. A conjugate base that spreads charge effectively is usually more stable than one that confines it to a small region, when other factors are comparable. A stable conjugate base corresponds to a stronger acid.
curriculum.reasoning: A carboxylate spreads negative charge over two oxygens through resonance. An ordinary alkoxide lacks that equivalent two-oxygen delocalisation. Nearby electron-withdrawing groups can also stabilise negative charge through inductive effects.
curriculum.worked_example: Compare CH3CO2H → CH3CO2− with CH3CH2OH → CH3CH2O−. The conjugate bases explain the large acidity difference.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Distance matters for induction, and geometry matters for resonance. The ability to draw an arrow does not prove that orbitals can overlap. Also compare electronegativity, atom size and solvent rather than using resonance as the only rule.

checks.question: Which species delocalises charge over two equivalent oxygens?
checks.explanation: The carboxylate has equivalent resonance contributors.

checks.question: An electron-withdrawing group often has what effect on a nearby conjugate anion?
checks.explanation: Electron withdrawal can disperse negative charge.

checks.question: Is drawing a resonance contributor enough without orbital overlap?
checks.explanation: Conjugation requires physically suitable orbital alignment.

curriculum.title: Donors meet acceptors
curriculum.question: Why is a strong base not always a fast nucleophile?
curriculum.plain_language: A nucleophile donates an electron pair to an electrophilic centre to form a bond. A base accepts a proton. The same reagent can do both, but the competition depends on what it attacks and on the reaction conditions.
curriculum.reasoning: Basicity describes an equilibrium tendency towards H+; nucleophilicity describes a reaction rate towards a particular electrophile. A bulky base may reach a small proton more easily than the crowded carbon required for substitution.
curriculum.worked_example: A bulky alkoxide may favour elimination from an alkyl halide. A less hindered nucleophile can favour SN2 at an accessible primary carbon.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Solvent, polarizability and the substrate change nucleophilicity. Never rank all nucleophiles using one universal list without specifying conditions. Decide between substitution and elimination by examining the whole reaction.

checks.question: Nucleophilicity is primarily a statement about what?
checks.explanation: It is a kinetic property for a defined reaction.

checks.question: Why can bulk encourage elimination over SN2?
options: A proton may be more accessible than carbon
checks.answer: A proton may be more accessible than carbon
checks.explanation: Steric access influences the competing pathways.

checks.question: Which site is electron-pair accepting in a simple carbonyl addition?
checks.explanation: Carbonyl carbon acts as the electrophile.

curriculum.title: Meet reactive intermediates
curriculum.question: Why does one missing bond change everything?
curriculum.plain_language: An intermediate is a species formed in one step and consumed in another. A carbocation has electron-deficient carbon; a carbanion has an electron pair associated with negatively charged carbon; a radical has an unpaired electron. They require different mechanistic reasoning.
curriculum.reasoning: Do not confuse an intermediate with a transition state. An intermediate corresponds to a local energy minimum and may have a finite lifetime. A transition state sits at the top of an elementary activation barrier.
curriculum.worked_example: An allylic carbocation spreads positive charge through a conjugated system. A simple SN2 reaction has a transition state but no carbocation intermediate.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Resonance, hyperconjugation, solvent and substituents influence stability. The familiar tertiary-over-secondary carbocation trend is useful for comparable simple alkyl cations; it is not a ranking that overrides every resonance effect.

checks.question: What distinguishes a radical?
checks.explanation: A radical has a singly occupied orbital.

checks.question: Where does an intermediate appear on a reaction-coordinate diagram?
checks.explanation: A minimum separates elementary-step barriers.

checks.question: Does an ordinary concerted SN2 form a carbocation intermediate?
checks.explanation: Bond formation and cleavage occur in one elementary step.

curriculum.title: Read an energy landscape
curriculum.question: Why can the more stable product form more slowly?
curriculum.plain_language: A reaction-coordinate diagram compares energy as a reaction progresses. It is not a graph of concentration against time. The activation free energy is the climb from a reactant state to its transition state; the reaction free energy compares products with reactants.
curriculum.reasoning: A smaller activation barrier generally gives a faster pathway under comparable conditions. A lower-energy product is thermodynamically favoured. These statements concern different energy differences and need not select the same product.
curriculum.worked_example: A fast-forming kinetic product may dominate when pathways are effectively irreversible. Equilibration can instead enrich the thermodynamically favoured product.
curriculum.advanced_connection: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower effective barrier. It does not change the equilibrium constant for the same overall reaction at the same temperature. Forward and reverse reactions are both accelerated.

checks.question: Which energy difference is most directly related to an elementary reaction rate?
checks.explanation: The barrier controls the rate constant.

checks.question: Does a catalyst change the equilibrium constant at fixed temperature?
checks.explanation: It changes the pathway, not the overall reaction free energy.

checks.question: The lowest-energy product must always form fastest. Is this true?
checks.explanation: Product stability and activation barriers are distinct.

curriculum.title: Rotate without reconnecting
curriculum.question: Can a molecule change shape without becoming a new compound?
curriculum.plain_language: Rotation about an ordinary single bond creates conformations while keeping connectivity unchanged. Use a Newman projection to look along a C–C bond: the front carbon is a point, and the rear carbon is shown as a circle.
curriculum.reasoning: Staggered ethane avoids the eclipsing alignment of C–H bonds. In butane, anti and gauche describe the relationship between its methyl groups. Comparing conformations requires both torsional and steric interactions.
curriculum.worked_example: For butane, anti places the two methyl groups approximately 180° apart; gauche places them approximately 60° apart in a staggered arrangement.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Conformations can influence which groups reach a reactive alignment. If conformers interconvert quickly, product ratios may depend on their reaction transition states rather than their populations alone.

checks.question: What changes during ordinary single-bond rotation?
checks.explanation: The same bonds connect the same atoms.

checks.question: In anti butane, methyl groups have approximately which dihedral angle?
checks.explanation: Anti means opposite in the Newman view.

checks.question: A Newman projection looks along what?
checks.explanation: It compares groups around the front and rear atoms.

curriculum.title: Ride the cyclohexane chair
curriculum.question: Why is a chair more useful than a flat hexagon?
curriculum.plain_language: Cyclohexane is not a flat regular hexagon. Its chair conformation keeps bond angles and torsional arrangements favourable. Each carbon has one axial and one equatorial bond to a substituent or hydrogen.
curriculum.reasoning: A chair flip exchanges axial and equatorial positions but preserves whether each substituent points up or down. Therefore a chair flip does not change cis into trans. A bulky group often prefers an equatorial position to reduce 1,3-diaxial interactions.
curriculum.worked_example: Methylcyclohexane can flip between axial-methyl and equatorial-methyl chairs. Its connectivity and up/down identity remain unchanged.
curriculum.advanced_connection: E2 elimination in a cyclohexane chair commonly requires a trans-diaxial leaving group and beta hydrogen. The more populated chair is not automatically the reactive chair.

checks.question: What happens to an axial substituent during a chair flip?
options: It necessarily changes cis to trans
It becomes equatorial with up/down retained
checks.answer: It becomes equatorial with up/down retained
checks.explanation: A chair flip changes conformation, not configuration.

checks.question: Why does a bulky methyl group often prefer equatorial placement?
checks.explanation: Equatorial placement reduces specific steric interactions.

checks.question: A cyclohexane E2 often needs which arrangement?
checks.explanation: This geometry supplies the required antiperiplanar alignment.

curriculum.title: Recognise mirror-image molecules
curriculum.question: When are a molecule and its mirror image different?
curriculum.plain_language: A chiral object cannot be superimposed on its mirror image. A tetrahedral carbon bearing four different groups is a common stereogenic centre. Its two mirror-image configurations can be enantiomers when the complete molecules are nonsuperimposable.
curriculum.reasoning: A wedge projects towards you and a dashed bond projects away. Rotating an entire molecule in space does not invert its configuration. Exchanging two groups at a single tetrahedral centre does invert it.
curriculum.worked_example: A carbon bonded to H, OH, CH3 and CH2CH3 has four different groups. A carbon bearing two identical methyl groups does not meet this tetrahedral criterion.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Counting stereocentres alone does not determine chirality. Internal symmetry can make a meso compound achiral, and other forms of chirality exist without an ordinary tetrahedral stereocentre.

checks.question: Which set can make a tetrahedral carbon stereogenic?
checks.explanation: Four distinguishable substituents allow two configurations.

checks.question: Does rotating a molecule as a whole change its configuration?
checks.explanation: Spatial rotation preserves the arrangement of bonded groups.

checks.question: Can a compound with stereocentres still be achiral?
options: Only if it has no atoms
Yes, for example a meso compound
checks.answer: Yes, for example a meso compound
checks.explanation: Molecular symmetry must also be considered.

curriculum.title: Assign R, S, E and Z
curriculum.question: Are these labels the same as clockwise rotation of light?
curriculum.plain_language: R and S describe configuration using Cahn–Ingold–Prelog priorities. Rank the groups, orient the lowest-priority group away and follow 1 → 2 → 3. Clockwise gives R in that view; anticlockwise gives S.
curriculum.reasoning: For E/Z, rank the two groups on each alkene carbon separately. Higher-priority groups on the same side give Z; on opposite sides give E. Each alkene carbon must have two different groups for this assignment.
curriculum.worked_example: On a tetrahedral centre, O outranks C at the first point of comparison because oxygen has higher atomic number. For isotopes of one element, higher mass number has higher priority.
curriculum.advanced_connection: R/S does not predict the sign of optical rotation. Also, an inversion of geometry need not always change the letter R to S if priorities change during a reaction. Track spatial arrangement and priorities separately.

checks.question: With group 4 pointing away, clockwise 1→2→3 gives what?
checks.explanation: That is the R configuration in the specified view.

checks.question: Higher-priority alkene groups on the same side give what?
checks.explanation: Z is assigned from the highest-priority groups on each end.

checks.question: Does R automatically mean positive optical rotation?
checks.explanation: Configuration and measured optical rotation are different properties.

curriculum.title: Equivalent on paper, different in a spectrum
curriculum.question: Can two hydrogens on the same carbon behave differently?
curriculum.plain_language: Two hydrogens on one carbon need not be chemically equivalent. Imagine replacing each hydrogen, one at a time, with a test group. Compare the two products: identical, enantiomeric or diastereomeric.
curriculum.reasoning: Identical products identify homotopic hydrogens; enantiomeric products identify enantiotopic hydrogens; diastereomeric products identify diastereotopic hydrogens. In an ordinary achiral medium, enantiotopic hydrogens generally share a chemical shift, while diastereotopic ones can differ.
curriculum.worked_example: A CH2 group next to an existing stereocentre can have diastereotopic hydrogens. The substitution test explains why separate resonances may appear.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Chemical equivalence is not identical to magnetic equivalence. Conformational averaging and chiral environments can alter observed behaviour. Do not predict one NMR signal simply because hydrogens are attached to one carbon.

checks.question: Replacing each H separately gives diastereomers. The H atoms are what?
checks.explanation: The replacement test defines diastereotopicity.

checks.question: Are all hydrogens on a CH2 group necessarily equivalent?
checks.explanation: Their molecular and stereochemical environments matter.

checks.question: Enantiotopic H atoms generally have which shifts in an achiral medium?
checks.explanation: An achiral medium generally does not distinguish enantiotopic sites.

curriculum.title: SN2: one coordinated exchange
curriculum.question: How does carbon change partners without stopping halfway?
curriculum.plain_language: In SN2 substitution, a nucleophile forms a bond as the leaving group departs. These events belong to one elementary step. At a stereogenic reacting carbon, backside attack inverts the spatial arrangement. There is no free carbocation waiting between the two events.
curriculum.reasoning: Draw the donor lone pair towards carbon and the C–leaving-group bonding pair towards the leaving group. Less crowded substrates are generally more accessible. The elementary rate law contains both substrate and nucleophile concentrations.
curriculum.worked_example: HO− + CH3Br → CH3OH + Br−. For this simple methyl example there is no stereocentre, but the concerted electron flow is the same.
curriculum.advanced_connection: The transition state has partially forming and breaking bonds; it is not a stable pentavalent carbon compound. Solvent and nucleophile influence the barrier. At a stereocentre, geometric inversion and the final R/S label must be checked separately.

checks.question: How many elementary steps describe the basic SN2 event?
checks.explanation: Formation and cleavage occur in one concerted event.

checks.question: What is the elementary SN2 rate law?
checks.explanation: Both reacting partners participate in the elementary step.

checks.question: At a reacting stereocentre, backside SN2 attack gives what?
checks.explanation: Backside displacement inverts the local spatial arrangement.

curriculum.title: SN1: a leaving group goes first
curriculum.question: Why can water substitute even though it is a weak nucleophile?
curriculum.plain_language: In the simplified SN1 pathway, the leaving group departs before the nucleophile attacks. A sufficiently stabilised carbocation can form, then react with water or another nucleophile. If a neutral nucleophile becomes positively charged on bonding, a deprotonation step may follow.
curriculum.reasoning: Ionisation often controls the rate, so the elementary teaching model gives rate = k[substrate]. Polar ionising media and stabilised carbocations can help. Primary alkyl substrates generally do not favour ordinary SN1 solvolysis.
curriculum.worked_example: tert-Butyl halide in an appropriate aqueous ionising medium can form tert-butanol through ionisation, water attack and deprotonation.
curriculum.advanced_connection: A planar carbocation permits attack from both faces, but real SN1 reactions need not give an exact 50:50 enantiomer mixture. Ion pairs and solvent cages can bias attack. Rearrangement and elimination may compete.

checks.question: What distinguishes the basic SN1 sequence?
options: All bonds change in one SN2 step
checks.explanation: A carbocation or closely associated ion-pair pathway is involved.

checks.question: The simplified SN1 rate law primarily depends on what?
checks.explanation: Rate-limiting ionisation gives the first-order model.

checks.question: Must every chiral SN1 reaction produce exactly 50:50 enantiomers?
checks.explanation: Ion-pair and solvent effects can bias the product mixture.

curriculum.title: E2: remove and release together
curriculum.question: Why does the direction of a hydrogen matter?
curriculum.plain_language: In E2 elimination, a base removes a beta hydrogen while a leaving group departs and a C=C bond forms. These changes occur in one elementary step. The hydrogen must be on a carbon adjacent to the leaving-group-bearing carbon.
curriculum.reasoning: Draw three electron-pair arrows: base to H; C–H bond to the new C=C bond; C–leaving-group bond to the leaving group. An antiperiplanar H–C–C–leaving-group arrangement commonly provides favourable orbital alignment.
curriculum.worked_example: A suitable base can eliminate HBr from bromoethane to give ethene. In a cyclohexane chair, look for the corresponding trans-diaxial arrangement.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Accessible beta hydrogens, substrate conformation and base size influence the product. More substituted alkenes often dominate with small bases, but steric and stereoelectronic constraints can override this shortcut.

checks.question: An E2 beta hydrogen sits where?
options: On a carbon adjacent to the leaving-group carbon
checks.answer: On a carbon adjacent to the leaving-group carbon
checks.explanation: Beta identifies the adjacent carbon position.

checks.question: Which alignment commonly favours E2?
checks.explanation: Alignment allows donation into the breaking-bond system.

checks.question: How many coordinated electron-pair arrows show the standard E2 event?
checks.explanation: Proton removal, pi-bond formation and leaving-group departure are coupled.

curriculum.title: E1: eliminate after ionisation
curriculum.question: What can a carbocation do besides accept a nucleophile?
curriculum.plain_language: A carbocation can lose a beta proton to form an alkene. In an E1 pathway, ionisation happens first, then a base removes that proton. The C–H bonding electrons supply the new pi bond.
curriculum.reasoning: E1 and SN1 can share a carbocation intermediate. Nucleophilic capture gives substitution; beta deprotonation gives elimination. The substrate, solvent and temperature influence their competition. Rearrangements may happen before either final step.
curriculum.worked_example: Acid-catalysed dehydration of an appropriate tertiary alcohol can involve water departure, a carbocation and beta deprotonation.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Do not impose the same concerted geometric demand on a free E1 carbocation as on an E2 transition state. Nevertheless, a suitable beta hydrogen and orbital alignment for alkene formation are still necessary.

checks.question: Which event follows carbocation formation in E1?
checks.explanation: The C–H pair forms the new pi bond.

checks.question: Which substitution pathway may share an intermediate with E1?
checks.explanation: Both can proceed through a carbocation.

checks.question: Can rearrangement compete in a carbocation-based E1 pathway?
options: Only after the alkene is isolated
checks.explanation: The cation may rearrange before elimination.

curriculum.title: Choose a pathway, not a slogan
curriculum.question: Why does the same halide give different products in different solvents?
curriculum.plain_language: Start with the substrate: methyl, primary, secondary or tertiary; allylic and benzylic systems deserve special attention. Then inspect nucleophile/basicity, steric bulk, solvent, leaving group and accessible beta hydrogens. A reaction label is a conclusion reached from this evidence.
curriculum.reasoning: SN2 needs an accessible carbon; ordinary SN1 needs feasible ionisation. E2 needs a base and a suitable beta hydrogen. E1 needs a feasible cation pathway. Secondary substrates often sit at the intersection of competing possibilities.
curriculum.worked_example: A tertiary alkyl halide is sterically unsuitable for normal SN2, but can undergo E2 with a strong base or solvolysis under suitable ionising conditions.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Mechanism predictions can remain conditional when concentrations or solvents are missing. Explain the assumptions and possible competing products instead of forcing one answer. Compare transition-state barriers rather than product names alone.

checks.question: Which observation argues strongly against ordinary SN2?
checks.explanation: Steric crowding blocks the normal backside pathway.

checks.question: What extra structural feature is needed for ordinary E2?
checks.explanation: Elimination needs a hydrogen on an appropriate adjacent carbon.

checks.question: If solvent and reagent details are missing, what is best?
checks.explanation: Incomplete conditions can make predictions genuinely ambiguous.

curriculum.title: Add HBr to an alkene
curriculum.question: Why does the proton choose one end of the double bond?
curriculum.plain_language: In an ordinary ionic HBr addition, the alkene pi pair accepts a proton and a carbocation-like intermediate forms. Bromide then attacks the electron-deficient carbon. Choose the initial protonation by comparing the intermediate pathways, not by memorising an unexplained arrow.
curriculum.reasoning: For a simple unsymmetrical alkene, protonation that leads to the more stabilised carbocation commonly dominates. This gives the familiar Markovnikov pattern. Resonance and substrate structure can change the simple alkyl comparison.
curriculum.worked_example: Propene + HBr, under ordinary ionic conditions, mainly gives 2-bromopropane through the secondary rather than primary carbocation pathway.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Carbocation rearrangements and competing reactions may occur. Radical HBr addition in the presence of appropriate initiators is a different mechanism and must be analysed separately.

checks.question: Which electrons attack H+ initially in ionic alkene addition?
options: A new lone pair on hydrogen
checks.explanation: The alkene acts as an electron-pair donor.

checks.question: For ordinary ionic HBr addition to propene, the major simple product is what?
checks.explanation: The preferred carbocation pathway leads to the secondary bromide.

checks.question: Can carbocation rearrangement occur in an appropriate ionic addition?
checks.explanation: A sufficiently long-lived cation can rearrange.

curriculum.title: A bromonium bridge
curriculum.question: Why do two bromines often approach from opposite faces?
curriculum.plain_language: An alkene can polarise Br2 and form a bridged bromonium ion. This three-membered intermediate helps explain why the reaction does not behave like unrestricted attack on a freely rotating, open carbocation.
curriculum.reasoning: Bromide opens the bridge by attacking from the face opposite the bridging bromine. The resulting vicinal dibromide has the characteristic anti-addition relationship. Use a three-dimensional drawing to follow which face is blocked.
curriculum.worked_example: Ethene + Br2 in a suitable non-nucleophilic medium gives 1,2-dibromoethane. A substituted alkene reveals the stereochemical information more clearly.
curriculum.advanced_connection: In water, solvent can compete with bromide and produce a bromohydrin. Conditions determine the trapping nucleophile. Do not use a dibromide outcome automatically for every bromination medium.

checks.question: Which intermediate explains ordinary alkene bromination?
checks.explanation: A three-membered bridge controls approach geometry.

checks.question: Bromide usually opens the bromonium bridge from which face?
checks.explanation: Backside opening produces anti addition.

checks.question: In aqueous bromination, which reagent can trap the intermediate?
checks.explanation: Water can compete and lead to a bromohydrin.

curriculum.title: Turn an alkene into an alcohol
curriculum.question: Why does water need help to add across C=C?
curriculum.plain_language: In acid-catalysed hydration, protonation activates the alkene. Water attacks a feasible carbocation, forming an oxonium ion. Removal of a proton then gives the alcohol and regenerates the acid catalyst.
curriculum.reasoning: Follow charge explicitly: neutral water becomes positively charged when it forms a third oxygen bond, then deprotonation restores neutral oxygen. A curved arrow begins at a water lone pair during the attack step.
curriculum.worked_example: Acid-catalysed hydration of propene gives mainly propan-2-ol under suitable conditions. Count the C, O and H atoms to check the net addition of water.
curriculum.advanced_connection: This carbocation-based route can rearrange and is reversible. Other hydration methods provide different selectivity or avoid a free carbocation. Reagent choice is part of the mechanism, not a decoration above the arrow.

checks.question: After neutral water attacks a carbocation, oxygen initially becomes what?
checks.explanation: Three ordinary bonds give the attacking oxygen formal +1 charge.

checks.question: Which final step commonly gives the neutral alcohol?
checks.explanation: Removing H+ returns oxygen to its neutral valence pattern.

checks.question: Can ordinary acid-catalysed alkene hydration rearrange?
checks.explanation: Its carbocation pathway can permit rearrangement.

curriculum.title: Hydroboration changes the route
curriculum.question: How can an alkene give the less substituted alcohol?
curriculum.plain_language: Hydroboration adds B and H across an alkene through a concerted pathway. They add to the same face. For a simple unsymmetrical alkene, boron generally attaches to the less substituted carbon; oxidation subsequently replaces C–B with C–O.
curriculum.reasoning: The usual hydroboration–oxidation sequence therefore gives an anti-Markovnikov alcohol overall, with syn addition of H and OH. It avoids the free carbocation involved in ordinary acid hydration.
curriculum.worked_example: Propene → organoborane → propan-1-ol after peroxide/base oxidation. The two operations must both be included in the reaction sequence.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Regioselectivity reflects steric and electronic effects in the transition state. Oxidation proceeds with retention at the migrating carbon. Do not apply the simple trend without checking unusual substrates and the particular borane.

checks.question: In simple hydroboration, B and H add with which relationship?
checks.explanation: The concerted pathway delivers both to the same face.

checks.question: Hydroboration–oxidation of propene mainly gives which simple alcohol?
checks.explanation: Boron enters the less substituted end and is replaced by OH.

checks.question: Does the standard hydroboration step require a free carbocation?
checks.explanation: It follows a concerted pathway.

curriculum.title: Follow one electron at a time
curriculum.question: Why do peroxides change HBr addition but not every HX addition?
curriculum.plain_language: Radical mechanisms use single-electron steps. Under suitable initiation conditions, radicals derived from a peroxide can generate Br radicals from HBr. A Br radical adds to the alkene, leaving a carbon radical that abstracts H from another HBr molecule.
curriculum.reasoning: The propagation sequence regenerates Br radical. For a simple unsymmetrical alkene, the route favouring the more stabilised carbon radical commonly leads to anti-Markovnikov HBr addition. Draw fishhook arrows for single-electron movement.
curriculum.worked_example: For propene under appropriate radical HBr conditions, addition commonly gives 1-bromopropane rather than the ordinary ionic major product.
curriculum.advanced_connection: A viable chain needs energetically suitable propagation steps. The familiar peroxide effect cannot simply be transferred to HCl or HI. Termination consumes radicals without propagating the chain.

checks.question: Which arrow represents a radical electron movement?
checks.explanation: A fishhook follows one electron.

checks.question: What makes a step part of chain propagation?
checks.explanation: A chain carrier is produced again.

checks.question: Can the HBr peroxide effect be assumed for every HX reagent?
options: Only if the alkene is small
checks.explanation: Propagation energetics differ for different hydrogen halides.

curriculum.title: Aromaticity is an electron pattern
curriculum.question: Can a seven-membered ring be aromatic?
curriculum.plain_language: Aromaticity is not a prize reserved for hexagons. For the simple Hückel systems studied here, look for a cyclic, approximately planar, continuously conjugated p-orbital system containing 4n+2 pi electrons. Ring atoms and pi electrons are different counts.
curriculum.reasoning: Benzene has six pi electrons. Tropylium, C7H7+, also has six pi electrons distributed around a seven-carbon ring. Neutral cycloheptatriene has an sp3 CH2 carbon that interrupts the continuous p system and is nonaromatic.
curriculum.worked_example: The cyclopentadienyl anion has four pi electrons from two double bonds plus two from a p-orbital lone pair: six pi electrons in five ring positions.
curriculum.advanced_connection: A planar, continuously conjugated 4n-electron cycle is antiaromatic in this model. A molecule can avoid antiaromaticity by becoming nonplanar. Apply these rules within their intended class of systems, not to every possible excited or polycyclic molecule.

checks.question: How many pi electrons does the tropylium cation contain?
checks.explanation: Its positive centre contributes an empty p orbital to a six-electron conjugated ring.

checks.question: Why is neutral cycloheptatriene nonaromatic?
options: Seven-membered rings can never be aromatic
Its sp3 CH2 interrupts cyclic conjugation
checks.answer: Its sp3 CH2 interrupts cyclic conjugation
checks.explanation: Continuous p overlap is missing at the saturated carbon.

checks.question: Which count fits the simple Hückel aromatic rule?
options: Every even number regardless of geometry
checks.explanation: Electron count must be combined with geometry and conjugation.

curriculum.title: Lose aromaticity, then win it back
curriculum.question: Why does benzene replace H instead of simply adding?
curriculum.plain_language: In electrophilic aromatic substitution, the ring donates a pi pair to an electrophile. The first bond-forming step gives a sigma complex whose cyclic aromatic conjugation is interrupted. Removing H+ from the substituted carbon then restores the pi system.
curriculum.reasoning: For nitration, protonation of nitric acid followed by water loss generates NO2+. Ring attack forms a C–N bond; an N=O pi pair shifts towards oxygen to preserve nitrogen’s octet. Deprotonation supplies the ring pi bond that restores aromaticity.
curriculum.worked_example: C6H6 + HNO3 → C6H5NO2 + H2O with sulfuric-acid activation. The net result replaces a ring hydrogen with NO2.
curriculum.advanced_connection: The sigma complex has resonance contributors, not several separate intermediates switching identities. Aromatic stabilisation helps explain the substitution pathway, but reagents, barriers and competing pathways still determine what occurs.

checks.question: What is the electrophile in ordinary mixed-acid nitration?
checks.explanation: Nitric acid activation generates nitronium.

checks.question: Which stage restores aromaticity?
checks.explanation: The C–H pair forms a new ring pi bond.

checks.question: Is the sigma complex still fully aromatic?
options: Only because it has a positive charge
checks.explanation: The substituted carbon temporarily interrupts cyclic conjugation.

curriculum.title: Read the ring’s existing substituent
curriculum.question: Why can a group slow a reaction but still direct it ortho and para?
curriculum.plain_language: A substituent can change both the overall reaction rate and the relative ease of attack at different positions. These are separate questions. Electron donation or withdrawal affects ring reactivity, while the intermediate pathways help explain orientation.
curriculum.reasoning: Halogens withdraw inductively and generally deactivate benzene towards electrophilic substitution. Their lone pairs can donate by resonance, relatively supporting ortho and para sigma-complex pathways. Thus deactivation and ortho/para direction can coexist.
curriculum.worked_example: Nitro groups commonly deactivate and direct meta. Alkyl groups commonly activate and direct ortho/para. Halogens are a useful exception to an oversimplified activation slogan.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Protonation can alter a substituent’s directing behaviour: an amino group in strongly acidic medium may become an ammonium group. Steric effects also influence ratios. A directing rule is not a complete quantitative product distribution.

checks.question: Halogens on benzene are generally what in electrophilic substitution?
checks.explanation: Induction and resonance affect different comparisons.

checks.question: A nitro substituent commonly directs a new electrophile where?
checks.explanation: Electron withdrawal disfavors particular sigma-complex pathways.

checks.question: Can protonating an amino substituent alter directing behaviour?
options: Only if its carbon skeleton changes
checks.explanation: Protonation changes its electron-donating ability.

curriculum.title: Aromatic substitution can be nucleophilic
curriculum.question: Why can a nitro group help replace an aryl halide?
curriculum.plain_language: An aryl halide does not normally undergo the simple backside SN2 of a primary alkyl halide. An activated aryl system can instead react by nucleophilic aromatic substitution through addition followed by elimination.
curriculum.reasoning: An electron-withdrawing group such as nitro, placed ortho or para to the leaving group, can stabilise the anionic addition intermediate by conjugation. Elimination of halide restores aromaticity. Identify activation before applying this mechanism.
curriculum.worked_example: An appropriately activated nitroaryl halide can react with hydroxide to give a nitrophenol after workup. The nitro position matters to the conjugated anion pathway.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Leaving-group trends for addition-limited SNAr need not match alkyl substitution trends. Other nucleophilic aromatic mechanisms also exist. Conditions and intermediate evidence distinguish the pathways.

checks.question: The classical activated SNAr pathway often follows which sequence?
checks.explanation: An anionic addition intermediate precedes aromaticity-restoring elimination.

checks.question: Where can nitro most directly stabilise this intermediate relative to the leaving group?
checks.explanation: These positions allow conjugative stabilisation of the anionic intermediate.

checks.question: Should alkyl SN2 leaving-group rules be transferred blindly to SNAr?
checks.explanation: The controlling elementary steps are different.

curriculum.title: Benzyne takes a different exit
curriculum.question: How can an aryl halide react without a nitro activator?
curriculum.plain_language: Under suitably strong basic conditions, some aryl halides can eliminate an adjacent proton and a leaving group to form a benzyne intermediate. A nucleophile then adds, and protonation gives the substituted aromatic product.
curriculum.reasoning: This is an elimination–addition pathway, distinct from activated addition–elimination SNAr. The strained benzyne bond is not an ordinary freely drawn alkyne. Check that an appropriate ortho hydrogen is available.
curriculum.worked_example: Chlorobenzene with sodium amide under suitable liquid-ammonia conditions is a classical benzyne-route example leading to aniline after protonation.
curriculum.advanced_connection: A nucleophile can add at either end of an unsymmetrical benzyne, so regioisomer mixtures may result. Isotopic labelling and substitution patterns can provide evidence that separates this pathway from alternatives.

checks.question: What is the defining order in the benzyne pathway?
checks.explanation: Formation of benzyne precedes nucleophile capture.

checks.question: Which structural requirement matters in the classical elimination?
checks.explanation: Elimination removes a neighbouring proton and leaving group.

checks.question: Can an unsymmetrical benzyne give more than one regioisomer?
options: Only if it is nonaromatic before attack
checks.explanation: Either end may be attacked, depending on substitution and conditions.

curriculum.title: Open the carbonyl pi bond
curriculum.question: Why does a nucleophile attack carbon rather than oxygen?
curriculum.plain_language: In a simple aldehyde or ketone, C=O is polarised towards oxygen. A nucleophile donates a pair to carbon while the pi pair moves to oxygen. This produces a tetrahedral intermediate or adduct with an alkoxide-like oxygen.
curriculum.reasoning: Protonation of that oxygen can produce an alcohol. The order of activation and attack depends on conditions: an acid may activate the carbonyl for a weak neutral nucleophile, while a strong anionic nucleophile can attack an unprotonated carbonyl.
curriculum.worked_example: An aldehyde receiving a hydride equivalent, followed by protonation, becomes a primary alcohol. Track the C=O pair onto oxygen during the addition.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Steric crowding and electron donation by substituents help explain why comparable aldehydes are often more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition. Conjugation and reagent type can alter this comparison.

checks.question: Where does the carbonyl pi pair move during ordinary nucleophilic addition?
checks.explanation: Oxygen accepts the pi pair as carbon forms a new bond.

checks.question: The attacked carbon changes approximately from what geometry to what?
checks.explanation: Addition changes the carbonyl carbon’s bonding pattern.

checks.question: Why are comparable aldehydes often more reactive than ketones?
options: Less crowding and less alkyl donation
checks.answer: Less crowding and less alkyl donation
checks.explanation: Both steric and electronic effects can favour aldehyde attack.

curriculum.title: Hydride builds an alcohol
curriculum.question: Where does the new C–H bond come from?
curriculum.plain_language: Reagents such as sodium borohydride deliver a hydride equivalent to an aldehyde or ketone. Represent the addition with electron donation to carbon and movement of the carbonyl pi pair to oxygen. Proton transfer or workup then gives the alcohol.
curriculum.reasoning: An aldehyde commonly gives a primary alcohol; a ketone gives a secondary alcohol. These outcomes follow from the carbon groups already attached to the carbonyl carbon. The carbon skeleton is retained in this simple reduction.
curriculum.worked_example: Propanone → propan-2-ol. The former carbonyl carbon gains H and retains its two methyl groups.
curriculum.advanced_connection: A hydride equivalent transferred from a reagent is not the same as a free proton in solution. Reagent strength and functional-group compatibility control chemoselectivity; do not treat every hydride reagent as interchangeable.

checks.question: Simple ketone reduction normally gives which alcohol class?
checks.explanation: The carbonyl carbon already bears two carbon groups.

checks.question: What completes the alkoxide-to-alcohol conversion?
options: Addition of a second oxygen necessarily
checks.explanation: The negatively charged oxygen accepts H+.

checks.question: Is a hydride equivalent the same as a proton?
checks.explanation: Hydride carries an electron pair; a proton does not.

curriculum.title: Build a carbon–carbon bond
curriculum.question: How can a carbon atom behave like a nucleophile?
curriculum.plain_language: An organomagnesium reagent has a strongly polarised C–Mg bond. Its carbon can behave as a carbon nucleophile towards a carbonyl. Addition forms a new C–C bond, and protonation during workup gives an alcohol.
curriculum.reasoning: Count carbon groups at the attacked carbon to predict the alcohol class. Formaldehyde can give a primary alcohol, other aldehydes secondary alcohols and ketones tertiary alcohols. This assumes the usual simple substrates and workup.
curriculum.worked_example: CH3MgBr + CH3CHO, followed by protonating workup, gives propan-2-ol. The methyl reagent supplies the new carbon group.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Grignard reagents are strongly basic and are quenched by water and many protic functional groups. Plan the order of operations and protect incompatible groups where necessary. Carbon–carbon bond formation competes with acid–base chemistry.

checks.question: Which bond is created during a Grignard carbonyl addition?
checks.explanation: The reagent carbon bonds to the carbonyl carbon.

checks.question: What happens if a Grignard reagent encounters water prematurely?
options: It is quenched by proton transfer
checks.answer: It is quenched by proton transfer
checks.explanation: Strong basicity makes water incompatible before the intended addition.

checks.question: A simple ketone plus a Grignard reagent and workup usually gives what?
checks.explanation: The attacked carbon acquires a third carbon substituent.

curriculum.title: Exchange carbonyl oxygen for nitrogen
curriculum.question: Why does imine formation need carefully balanced acidity?
curriculum.plain_language: A primary amine can add to an aldehyde or ketone. Proton transfers give a carbinolamine; removal of water gives an iminium species, and deprotonation can give an imine. Think of addition followed by dehydration rather than a single unexplained oxygen-for-nitrogen swap.
curriculum.reasoning: Acid can assist carbonyl activation and water departure, but very strong protonation makes the amine less nucleophilic. The balance of activation, nucleophile availability and water removal affects conversion.
curriculum.worked_example: A simple aldehyde plus a primary amine can form R–CH=N–R′ plus water under suitable reversible dehydration conditions.
curriculum.advanced_connection: With suitable secondary amines and substrates bearing alpha hydrogens, enamine formation can occur instead. Imines and enamines become useful synthetic tools because their carbon and nitrogen reactivity differ from the starting carbonyl.

checks.question: What intermediate forms after amine addition and proton transfers?
checks.explanation: The same carbon temporarily bears OH and nitrogen.

checks.question: Why can too much acid slow nucleophilic amine attack?
options: It protonates the amine lone pair
checks.answer: It protonates the amine lone pair
checks.explanation: An ammonium nitrogen is much less available as a nucleophile.

checks.question: Which amine class commonly gives an imine from a simple carbonyl?
checks.explanation: A primary amine can condense to a C=N-containing imine.

curriculum.title: Addition or substitution at C=O?
curriculum.question: Why does an ester behave differently from a ketone?
curriculum.plain_language: An acyl compound can carry a substituent that leaves after nucleophilic attack. Addition first gives a tetrahedral intermediate; collapse then reforms C=O and can expel the leaving group. This is nucleophilic acyl substitution.
curriculum.reasoning: A simple aldehyde or ketone has no comparable heteroatom leaving group at its carbonyl carbon, so ordinary addition does not follow the same leaving-group pathway. Acyl chloride, ester and amide reactivity depends strongly on leaving-group ability and resonance donation.
curriculum.worked_example: An acyl chloride reacting with an alcohol can give an ester. An ester reacting with a suitable amine can give an amide under appropriate conditions.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Proton transfers and acidic or basic conditions change the details. An acyl substitution is not an SN2 attack at tetrahedral alkyl carbon. Distinguish which bond breaks and which carbon is attacked.

checks.question: What follows tetrahedral addition in an acyl substitution?
options: Permanent loss of the carbonyl carbon
checks.explanation: C=O reforms as a substituent leaves.

checks.question: Why does an ordinary ketone often undergo addition instead?
options: It lacks a comparable acyl leaving group
checks.answer: It lacks a comparable acyl leaving group
checks.explanation: The groups on carbon do not provide the usual heteroatom leaving group.

checks.question: Is acyl substitution the same elementary process as alkyl SN2?
checks.explanation: Their reaction centres and intermediate pathways differ.

curriculum.title: Borrow reactivity from the alpha carbon
curriculum.question: Why can a carbon next to C=O lose a proton?
curriculum.plain_language: The alpha carbon is directly next to a carbonyl carbon. Removing an alpha proton can give an enolate whose electrons are delocalised between carbon and oxygen. This makes some carbon-bound hydrogens much more acidic than those of ordinary alkanes.
curriculum.reasoning: Draw an arrow from base to H, the C–H pair towards the carbonyl carbon and the C=O pi pair towards oxygen. Carbon-centred and oxygen-centred contributors describe the same enolate, not independent compounds switching places.
curriculum.worked_example: A suitable base can remove an alpha H from propanone to form its enolate. Alkylation at carbon makes a new C–C bond.
curriculum.advanced_connection: An enolate is ambident: reaction may occur at carbon or oxygen depending on reagent and conditions. It is not an enol; an enol is a neutral C=C–OH tautomer with different proton connectivity.

checks.question: Where is an alpha carbon relative to C=O?
checks.explanation: Alpha identifies the neighbouring carbon position.

checks.question: Why is an enolate stabilised relative to a simple localised alkyl anion?
checks.explanation: Conjugation distributes the electron density.

checks.question: Is an enolate identical to a neutral enol?
checks.explanation: Charge and proton connectivity distinguish them.

curriculum.title: Choose kinetic or thermodynamic control
curriculum.question: Can the faster proton removal give the less stable enolate?
curriculum.plain_language: An unsymmetrical ketone may have alpha hydrogens on either side. Different deprotonation pathways can produce different enolates. The kinetic product forms through the lower accessible barrier; the thermodynamic product is favoured after appropriate equilibration.
curriculum.reasoning: A bulky strong base at low temperature can favour removal of a more accessible proton under kinetic conditions. Reversible conditions may instead favour the more stable enolate. These are useful patterns, not guarantees independent of solvent and substrate.
curriculum.worked_example: For an unsymmetrical ketone, draw both possible enolates first. Compare access to each proton and the stability of each delocalised product before choosing conditions.
curriculum.advanced_connection: To justify a selection, specify base, temperature, solvent, addition order and reversibility. A reaction drawing that omits them may not determine one enolate uniquely.

checks.question: A kinetic enolate is selected mainly by what?
checks.explanation: Kinetic control compares activation barriers.

checks.question: What enables thermodynamic product selection?
options: A guarantee that every reaction is reversible
checks.explanation: Reversibility allows interconversion towards a lower-energy distribution.

checks.question: Should one enolate be asserted without base or temperature information?
options: Only if the ketone is large
checks.explanation: Important selectivity conditions may be missing.

curriculum.title: Aldol joins two carbonyl stories
curriculum.question: How can one carbonyl compound attack another?
curriculum.plain_language: An enolate can donate from its alpha carbon to the carbonyl carbon of another molecule. The attacked C=O pair moves to oxygen. Protonation gives a beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound: the aldol addition product.
curriculum.reasoning: The donor retains its carbonyl, while its alpha carbon forms the new C–C bond. The acceptor’s carbonyl becomes the alcohol-bearing carbon. Dehydration can subsequently form a conjugated alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl under suitable conditions.
curriculum.worked_example: Two ethanal molecules can give 3-hydroxybutanal by aldol addition. Loss of water then gives but-2-enal under suitable dehydration conditions.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Addition and condensation are different stages. Crossed aldol reactions can give mixtures unless donor and acceptor roles are controlled. Enolate geometry and transition-state organisation influence stereochemistry.

checks.question: Which atoms form the new bond in an aldol addition?
options: Enolate alpha carbon and acceptor carbonyl carbon
checks.answer: Enolate alpha carbon and acceptor carbonyl carbon
checks.explanation: Carbon nucleophilicity joins the carbonyl partners.

checks.question: The immediate protonated aldol addition product contains what?
checks.explanation: The acceptor carbonyl becomes an OH-bearing carbon.

checks.question: Does every aldol addition automatically include dehydration?
options: Only if the donor is an aldehyde
checks.explanation: Condensation adds a separate water-loss stage.

curriculum.title: Claisen condensation makes a beta-keto ester
curriculum.question: Why does ester condensation need a base and a final workup?
curriculum.plain_language: An ester enolate can attack another ester’s carbonyl. A tetrahedral intermediate forms and then expels alkoxide, restoring C=O. The product has a beta-keto ester arrangement rather than the beta-hydroxy structure of an aldol addition.
curriculum.reasoning: The beta-dicarbonyl product can be deprotonated readily, helping drive the classical Claisen equilibrium. Acidic workup returns its neutral form. A compatible alkoxide base can reduce competing ester exchange.
curriculum.worked_example: Ethyl acetate can undergo a classical Claisen condensation with ethoxide, followed by acidic workup, to form ethyl acetoacetate.
curriculum.advanced_connection: The classical self-Claisen requires a suitable alpha-hydrogen pattern so product deprotonation can provide a driving force. Crossed and intramolecular variants demand additional substrate planning.

checks.question: Which functional arrangement characterises a simple Claisen product?
checks.explanation: Acyl substitution joins ester-derived carbon fragments.

checks.question: What can help drive the classical reaction?
checks.explanation: Product deprotonation pulls the equilibrium.

checks.question: Why choose an alkoxide matching the ester’s alkoxy group?
checks.explanation: Compatible alkoxide helps avoid transesterification mixtures.

curriculum.title: Michael addition looks further away
curriculum.question: Why can a nucleophile attack beyond the carbonyl carbon?
curriculum.plain_language: An alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl is a conjugated system. Its beta carbon can accept nucleophilic attack through a conjugate-addition pathway. Donation at beta shifts the pi system to an enolate-like intermediate, which is then protonated.
curriculum.reasoning: Compare 1,2 addition at the carbonyl with 1,4 addition across the conjugated system. A Michael reaction commonly joins an appropriate stabilised carbon nucleophile to a conjugated acceptor. Reagent identity controls which pathway is favoured.
curriculum.worked_example: An appropriate enolate adds to the beta carbon of an enone. A protonated conjugate-addition product retains a carbonyl group.
curriculum.advanced_connection: A Michael addition followed by an intramolecular aldol condensation forms the core sequence of a Robinson annulation. Track atoms to explain the resulting ring, rather than treating the named reaction as a memorised product stencil.

checks.question: A simple Michael donor commonly attacks which position of an enone?
options: A remote saturated methyl group necessarily
checks.explanation: Conjugation allows beta electrophilicity.

checks.question: Which two additions should be compared for a conjugated carbonyl?
checks.explanation: The reagent can select carbonyl or conjugate attack.

checks.question: A Robinson annulation combines Michael addition with what?
checks.explanation: The linked sequence builds a ring.

curriculum.title: Oxidise an alcohol with purpose
curriculum.question: Why can one alcohol become an aldehyde and another a ketone?
curriculum.plain_language: Oxidising an alcohol commonly increases bonding from its carbon to oxygen while removing hydrogen equivalents. A primary alcohol can lead to an aldehyde, and further oxidation may give a carboxylic acid. A secondary alcohol commonly gives a ketone.
curriculum.reasoning: The outcome depends on reagent and conditions. A primary alcohol does not stop automatically at an aldehyde with every oxidant. A tertiary alcohol lacks the usual hydrogen on its OH-bearing carbon for this simple oxidation pathway.
curriculum.worked_example: Ethanol → ethanal under aldehyde-preserving conditions; propan-2-ol → propanone under suitable oxidation conditions.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Think in oxidation-state changes and mechanistic activation rather than oxygen addition alone. Some alcohol oxidations proceed through reagent-bound oxygen intermediates followed by elimination-like bond changes.

checks.question: Simple oxidation of a secondary alcohol commonly gives what?
checks.explanation: The OH-bearing carbon becomes carbonyl carbon.

checks.question: Does every oxidant stop a primary alcohol at an aldehyde?
options: Only if it contains two carbons
checks.explanation: Reagent and medium determine further oxidation.

checks.question: Why does a tertiary alcohol resist the usual simple carbonyl-forming route?
options: Its OH-bearing carbon lacks a C–H bond
checks.answer: Its OH-bearing carbon lacks a C–H bond
checks.explanation: The conventional removal of hydrogen equivalents is unavailable at that centre.

curriculum.title: Reduce selectively
curriculum.question: How can one carbonyl react while another survives?
curriculum.plain_language: Chemoselectivity means choosing one functional group in the presence of another. A useful reagent does not merely make a product; it also leaves the groups you want to preserve. Compare the substrate’s entire list of reactive sites.
curriculum.reasoning: Sodium borohydride commonly reduces aldehydes and ketones under standard teaching conditions. Lithium aluminium hydride can reduce less reactive derivatives such as many esters and amides under appropriate conditions. Their handling and compatibility are different.
curriculum.worked_example: In a substrate containing a ketone and an ester, suitable borohydride conditions can reduce the ketone preferentially. Check the specific substrate and conditions.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Selectivity depends on conditions, reagent equivalents and substrate structure. Protection and later deprotection can be part of a synthesis, but they add operations and must be justified. Never assume a reagent recognises your intended target group.

checks.question: Chemoselectivity concerns choosing between what?
checks.explanation: It identifies which group reacts within a multifunctional substrate.

checks.question: Which reagent is commonly more broadly reducing towards esters and amides?
checks.explanation: Lithium aluminium hydride is a strong hydride reagent.

checks.question: Are equivalents and conditions relevant to selectivity?
checks.explanation: The same reagent can behave differently under different conditions.

curriculum.title: Baeyer–Villiger inserts oxygen
curriculum.question: How does a ketone become an ester without losing its carbon skeleton?
curriculum.plain_language: A peracid can add to a ketone and form a peroxide-containing tetrahedral intermediate. One adjacent carbon group then migrates to oxygen while the O–O bond breaks. The overall transformation inserts oxygen beside the original carbonyl carbon.
curriculum.reasoning: A cyclic ketone can therefore give a ring-expanded lactone. To analyse an unsymmetrical ketone, consider both possible migrating groups and the geometries that permit migration. Oxygen insertion does not mean a free oxygen atom wanders into a bond.
curriculum.worked_example: Cyclohexanone can undergo Baeyer–Villiger oxidation to a seven-membered lactone using suitable peracid conditions.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Migration involves the bonding pair and generally retains configuration at the migrating carbon. Migratory preference is influenced by electronic and stereoelectronic factors, so a single universal ranking is not a substitute for substrate analysis.

checks.question: A simple ketone undergoes which net transformation in Baeyer–Villiger oxidation?
checks.explanation: Oxygen is inserted adjacent to the carbonyl carbon.

checks.question: A cyclic ketone can give what?
checks.explanation: The inserted oxygen becomes a ring atom.

checks.question: During migration, does the migrating carbon normally retain its configuration?
options: It becomes a free carbocation first
checks.explanation: Migration carries the bonding pair in an organised rearrangement.

curriculum.title: Beckmann follows the group opposite
curriculum.question: Why does the oxime geometry decide which group migrates?
curriculum.plain_language: A ketoxime can rearrange to an amide after suitable activation of its hydroxyl group. In the standard Beckmann pathway, the group anti to the departing group migrates from carbon to nitrogen as the leaving group departs.
curriculum.reasoning: The resulting nitrilium intermediate is trapped and converted to the amide. Follow which carbon group moves: it becomes attached to nitrogen in the product. Different oxime geometries can therefore lead to different constitutional amides.
curriculum.worked_example: Cyclohexanone oxime can rearrange to caprolactam under appropriate activated conditions. The nitrogen becomes part of the expanded ring.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Stereoelectronic alignment is central, so a memorised migratory ranking alone can give the wrong product. Cyclic oximes can form ring-expanded lactams, connecting mechanism to industrial synthesis.

checks.question: Which group migrates in the standard Beckmann pathway?
options: The group anti to the leaving group
Always the smallest group regardless of geometry
checks.answer: The group anti to the leaving group
checks.explanation: Oxime geometry controls the required alignment.

checks.question: What product class forms from a ketoxime?
checks.explanation: Migration to nitrogen leads through a nitrilium pathway to an amide.

checks.question: A cyclic ketoxime may form what?
checks.explanation: The migrating ring bond incorporates nitrogen into the expanded ring.

curriculum.title: Pinacol moves a bond
curriculum.question: How can a diol rearrange into a carbonyl?
curriculum.plain_language: Under suitable acidic conditions, one hydroxyl group of a vicinal diol is activated and water departs. A neighbouring group can migrate with its bonding pair while the other oxygen forms a carbonyl bond. Deprotonation gives the neutral carbonyl product.
curriculum.reasoning: Track the migrating C–C or C–H bond, not a free wandering atom. The neighbouring oxygen helps stabilise the electron-deficient pathway. Substrate geometry and which hydroxyl group leaves influence the outcome.
curriculum.worked_example: Pinacol, a vicinal diol, rearranges to pinacolone under suitable acid conditions. Atom mapping reveals that a methyl group has changed its bonding partner.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Unsymmetrical substrates can offer several pathways. Cation stability, migration and stereoelectronic alignment must be considered together. The simple named-reaction label does not by itself determine one product.

checks.question: Which starting arrangement is characteristic of a pinacol rearrangement?
checks.explanation: The two adjacent OH-bearing carbons enable the rearrangement.

checks.question: What moves during a migration?
options: A group with its bonding electron pair
checks.answer: A group with its bonding electron pair
checks.explanation: Bond migration redistributes connectivity and electrons together.

checks.question: Why can an unsymmetrical substrate be challenging?
options: Several leaving and migrating pathways can compete
checks.answer: Several leaving and migrating pathways can compete
checks.explanation: The complete substrate and conditions determine selectivity.

curriculum.title: Meet HOMO and LUMO
curriculum.question: Why does a nucleophile need a suitable empty orbital?
curriculum.plain_language: An occupied orbital can donate into a suitable unoccupied orbital when energy and spatial overlap permit. HOMO means highest occupied molecular orbital; LUMO means lowest unoccupied molecular orbital. These labels help describe donor–acceptor interactions.
curriculum.reasoning: In a simple nucleophilic carbonyl addition, a donor orbital interacts with the carbonyl pi-star acceptor orbital. Approach direction matters because overlap is directional. Charges provide a useful clue, but orbitals help explain the geometry behind it.
curriculum.worked_example: A lone-pair donor can interact with an electrophile’s acceptor orbital. Rotating the approach can improve or spoil overlap even if the atoms remain close.
curriculum.advanced_connection: Orbital phase is the sign of a wavefunction, not an electrical charge painted on a lobe. Constructive overlap requires appropriate phase relationships. Frontier-orbital models simplify a larger electronic-structure problem.

checks.question: HOMO stands for what?
checks.explanation: It identifies the highest-energy occupied MO in the chosen model.

checks.question: A nucleophilic donor typically interacts with which type of orbital?
checks.explanation: Donation needs a suitable acceptor and spatial overlap.

checks.question: Does orbital phase mean positive or negative electrical charge?
checks.explanation: Phase is a wavefunction sign, not a charge label.

curriculum.title: Diels–Alder closes a six-membered ring
curriculum.question: How can two bonds form in one coordinated reaction?
curriculum.plain_language: A conjugated diene and a dienophile can combine in a [4+2] cycloaddition. Four diene pi electrons and two dienophile pi electrons participate. Two new sigma bonds form and one pi bond remains in the newly formed six-membered ring.
